classification.difficultyReason: Design a question and population within a supplied stepwise survey protocol, pilot it, choose random selection and compare sample proportions; the stages scaffold each familiar decision.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Write a yes/no question on a topic that interests you for a survey of a sample of 40 students.

answer.short: Sample answer: Do you usually walk to school?
answer.worked: Sample answer: “Do you usually walk to school?” This asks about one topic and allows a yes or no response.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Decide what population you will sample from. This could be all girls in Year 8, or students in Year 9, or boarders.

answer.short: Sample answer: All Year 8 students at my school.
answer.worked: Sample answer: The population is all Year 8 students at my school. The sample will contain 40 students selected from this population.

children.label: c
children.prompt: First, test your question on a small group of people.

answer.short: Sample answer: Five students understood the question and could answer yes or no.
answer.worked: Sample answer: Ask five students the question and check what they think it means. All five understood “usually” as their normal way of travelling to school, so no change was needed. Revise the wording if the pilot reveals confusion.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Decide on a method for random sampling. Use your method to select 40 students from your population, then ask them your question and record their responses.

answer.short: Sample answer: Number every Year 8 student and randomly select 40 different numbers. Survey those students and record their responses.
answer.worked: Sample answer: Give every Year 8 student a different number. Use a random number generator to select 40 different numbers from the complete list, ignoring repeats. Ask the selected students the same question and record each yes or no response.

children.label: e
children.prompt: Work out your sample proportion of a ‘yes’ response.

answer.short: Answers depend on the survey. Sample answer: $\frac{24}{40}=0.6=60\%$.
answer.worked:
Sample answer: Suppose 24 of the 40 students answered yes.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Sample proportion of yes responses}&=\frac{\text{number of yes responses}}{\text{sample size}}\\\text{Sample proportion of yes responses}&=\frac{24}{40}\\\text{Sample proportion of yes responses}&=0.6=60\%\end{align*}$$

inlines.text: Compare your sample proportion of a ‘yes’ response with the sample proportion that others obtained.
Each result is an estimate of the proportion of ‘yes’ responses for the population.

answer.short: Answers vary. Sample answer: Our proportion was 60%; another sample gave 55%. Ours was 5 percentage points higher.
answer.worked: Sample answer: For the same question and population, our sample gave 60% yes responses and another sample gave 55%. The difference is $60\%-55\%=5$ percentage points. Different random samples can give different proportions; each proportion estimates the population proportion.
